newsitem.title: USA: Dole launches 96-hour 'victory tour' to election.
newsitem.headline: Dole launches 96-hour 'victory tour' to election.

text.p: Republican Bob Dole on Friday launched his hectic 96-hour "victory tour" with a send-off by former Presidents George Bush and Gerald Ford in a bid to pull off a spectacular upset victory on Tuesday.

The marathon, stopping only for showers in hotels, will take Dole to at least 14 states before Election Day and test not only whether voters will oust President Bill Clinton from the White House but also the 73-year-old Dole's endurance.
"How do you feel?," Dole was asked as he left his hotel early on Friday for a rally at Capital University. "Feel great -- not so sure about tomorrow morning," he said.

By Saturday morning, Dole will have been up for most of that 24 hour period. After campaigning in Ohio during the day, he will go by bus through Michigan into the night and on to Detroit after midnight before heading to Newark, New Jersey, and Philadelphia as the sun rises.

Dole, lagging in polls, told the university rally his 96-hour campaign blitz was a serious effort. "We're not doing this to punish the media," he said in a lighthearted reference to his jibes against the "liberal media."
Both Ford and Bush shared the stage at the university and planned to travel with him to two other stops.
"We have four big days," Dole said. "We're going to win this election ... this is a fight for America, to elect a president we can trust, and one who will give us an economy that will give us hope."

But the thrust of his talk was a steady attack on alleged ethical lapses in the White House and controversy over questionable contributions to the Democratic Party from people with links to Indonesia, Taiwan and other foreign interests.

He noted that the Republicans had their Watergate scandal under President Richard Nixon and said the party had learned its lesson. "We took a licking, we reformed, but we didn't go far enough," Dole said.

Saying he understood Clinton would propose a bipartisan commission to overhaul campaign finance laws, Dole said this was an idea he had six years ago as a senator. "I suggested it again two weeks ago in New Hampshire -- so I'm glad the president's making progress," he said, calling on Clinton to accept "common sense ground rules" such as barring campaign contributions from non-Americans.

"The administration is in the midst of a growing scandal involving a flow of foreign money into the Democratic Party that bought access to the White House. So now Bill Clinton decides to talk about campaign finance reform," Dole said.
"What we have seen from this administration in the last few weeks is the reason we need campaign finance reform."
The Democratic National Committee and a chief fundraiser, John Huang, are under fire for accepting contributions from non-Americans.

Both Bush and Ford adopted the current Dole line of attack against alleged misdeeds in the White House. Bush mentioned the collection of sensitive FBI files on Republicans by Clinton White House security office aides, saying that when he was president he never saw an FBI file.
Ford urged voters to fight apathy and vote, saying if he had won Ohio -- a battleground state where Clinton leads -- he would have beaten Jimmy Carter for the presidency in 1976.

"I know Bob Dole to be a person of unquestioned integrity of the highest moral character," Ford said. "A Dole White House will be a drug-free White House. A Dole White House will not have big donor contributors running in and out on a daily basis."

From noon Friday to noon Tuesday, Dole promised to "give it all I got" to win an election that polls have made Clinton a heavy favourite to win. Dole's schedule takes him by bus and plane through the Midwest and East and then west to California before ending in his hometown, Russell, Kansas, to vote.
